A cooperative of 600 small coffee farmers in the hills above San Telmo is trying something its members have discussed for years: selling a growing share of its beans directly to roasters abroad, instead of through the exporters that have handled almost all of its crop since the 1990s.

The Alto Verde cooperative shipped its first two containers under the new arrangement last month, one to a roaster in Copenhagen and one to a group of cafés in Melbourne. Together they account for about a tenth of this year's harvest.

The move comes after two years in which the price paid for green coffee on international markets has swung wildly. Prices reached a record high early last year, then fell by almost a third in six months as a large harvest elsewhere came in.

"When the price falls, the exporter still makes a margin. The farmer is the one who absorbs it," said Gabriel Ruiz, the cooperative's general manager. "With a direct contract we agree a price for the season before the beans are picked. Our members can plan."

Under the contracts, roasters pay a fixed price per kilogram that is set above the market average of the past five years, plus a premium for beans that score highly in cupping tests. In return, the cooperative takes on the paperwork, shipping and quality control that exporters used to handle.

That has meant hiring. Alto Verde has taken on a logistics coordinator and two quality testers, and it has built a small laboratory next to its drying patios, where samples from every lot are roasted and tasted before shipping.

Not everyone is convinced. Some members worry that a single rejected container could wipe out the gains of a whole season. Economists who study farm cooperatives say the model works best when buyers commit for several years, which only a few of Alto Verde's new partners have done so far.

Ruiz says the cooperative will not abandon its exporters. "We are not burning any bridges," he said. "But if we can sell a third of our coffee this way within five years, our families will be far less exposed to a market none of us controls."
